title: Mockery about the mother of Jesus
source_text: Οὐ δοκεῖ μοι ἀγωνίσασθαι πρὸς λόγον, μὴ μετὰ σπουδῆς ἀλλὰ μετὰ χλεύης εἰρημένον· εἰ ἄρα καλὴ ἦν ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, καὶ ὡς καλῇ αὐτῇ ἐμίγνυτο ὁ θεὸς, οὐ πεφυκὼς ἐρᾶν φθαρτοῦ σώματος; ἢ ὅτι οὐδ᾿ εἰκὸς ἦν ἐρασθήσεσθαι αὐτῆς τὸν θεὸν, οὔσης οὔτ᾿ εὐδαίμονος οὔτε βασιλικῆς, ἐπεὶ μηδεὶς αὐτὴν ᾔδει μηδὲ τῶν γειτόνων· παίζει δὲ λέγων καὶ ὅτι μισουμένην αὐτὴν ὑπὸ τοῦ τέκτονος καὶ ἐκβαλλομένην οὐκ ἔσωσε θεία δύναμις οὐδὲ λόγος πιστικός. οὐδὲν οὖν, φησὶ, ταῦτα πρὸς τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ βασιλείαν. τί οὖν ταῦτα διαφέροι ἂν τῶν ἐν ταῖς τριόδοις λοιδορουμένων τισὶ καὶ οὐδὲν σπουδῆς ἄξιον λεγόντων;
pass_a_gloss: It does not seem [right] to me to contend (ἀγωνίσασθαι) against a statement (λόγος) said not with seriousness (σπουδή) but with mockery (χλεύη): whether then the mother of Jesus was beautiful (καλή), and as with a beautiful woman God had intercourse (ἐμίγνυτο) with her, not being by nature [disposed] (πεφυκώς) to love (ἐρᾶν) a corruptible body (φθαρτοῦ σώματος)? or that it was not even likely (εἰκός) that God would fall in love with her, she being neither prosperous (εὐδαίμονος) nor royal (βασιλικῆς), since no one knew her, not even of the neighbours; and he jests (παίζει) saying also that her, being hated by the carpenter (τέκτονος) and being cast out (ἐκβαλλομένην), divine power (θεία δύναμις) did not save, nor persuasive speech (λόγος πιστικός). Nothing, then, he says, are these things toward (i.e. relevant to) the kingdom of God (βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ). How then would these differ from [the words] of some who revile (λοιδορουμένων) at the crossroads (τρίοδοι) and say nothing worthy of seriousness?
pass_b_english: I do not think I need contend with an argument put forward not in earnest but in mockery: “Was the mother of Jesus beautiful, then, and did God have intercourse with her because she was beautiful, though it is not his nature to love a perishable body?” Or that “it was not even likely that God would fall in love with her, since she was neither wealthy nor of royal birth; for no one knew her, not even her neighbours.” He is joking too when he says that “when she was hated by the carpenter and driven out, neither divine power nor persuasive speech saved her.” “These things, then,” he says, “have nothing to do with the kingdom of God.” How would such remarks differ from those of people who hurl abuse at others at the crossroads and say nothing worth serious attention?

choices.choice: The phrases from εἰ ἄρα to the end of the 'carpenter' clause are Celsus's words (or his Jew's), partly as a question and partly in indirect speech; they are set in quotation marks. Whether 'though it is not his nature to love a perishable body' belongs to Celsus's question or to Origen's comment is not certain from the punctuation; it is taken with Celsus, as the participle agrees with ὁ θεός inside the question. εὐδαίμονος here means 'prosperous, wealthy' rather than 'happy'. λόγος πιστικός is taken as 'persuasive speech' (a convincing word to Joseph); 'trustworthy word' is possible. 'The carpenter' is Joseph; the slander of 1.28 and 1.32 (Mary driven out by her husband) is in view. No Scripture is quoted.
λοιδορουμένων τισί: 'hurl abuse at others' (was 'at one another', not in the Greek)
